claims.text: Resistance of HEAs to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by their ability to form a stable, self-healing passive film.
The mixture of alloying elements in HEAs promotes a uniform distribution of passive-film-forming species such as Cr and Al.
Passive-film-forming species preferentially concentrate at grain boundaries and defect sites.
The passive film protects the underlying HEA from corrosive attack.
The passive film rapidly regenerates after it is mechanically removed by wear.
The concentration of passive-film-forming elements can be changed between the enhanced and control alloys without significantly changing mechanical properties or grain structure.
A homogeneous distribution of passive-film-forming elements, particularly along grain boundaries and near defects, enables effective corrosion inhibition after mechanical disruption.
A well-distributed, stable, self-healing passive film limits both corrosion initiation and corrosion propagation.
A reservoir of passive-film-forming elements and a favorable microstructure permit rapid repassivation after wear damage.
Rapid repassivation prevents continuously compounded wear-corrosion degradation.
Under simultaneous wear-corrosion conditions, the enhanced HEA will have significantly lower overall mass loss than the control HEA.
The enhanced HEA will exhibit smaller corrosion-potential shifts than the control HEA.
The enhanced HEA will have lower individual wear and corrosion rates than the control HEA.
Reformation of the passive film will produce a synergistic reduction in combined degradation.
An HEA containing fewer passive-film-forming elements will form an inferior passive film under otherwise identical conditions.
The beneficial effect will hold when mechanical film removal is slower than the alloy's repassivation kinetics.
The beneficial effect may disappear when wear removes the film faster than it can reform.
Electrolytes sufficiently aggressive to disrupt passive-film formation may invalidate the predicted advantage.

contradictions.description: The passive-film-forming species are described as homogeneously or uniformly distributed while also being preferentially concentrated at grain boundaries and defect sites. These descriptions require clarification, such as distinguishing bulk homogeneity from controlled interfacial segregation.
